inline.s: The patriarchs were the masters who transmitted the Buddha's mind-seal, one to another. It is said that when the World-Honored One taught on Vulture Peak, twelve hundred and fifty disciples always followed him; and when at the last he held up a flower, Kāśyapa broke into a smile and received the mind-seal. Thus was established the purport of a transmission apart from the teachings, which became the Chan school. Through twenty-eight generations it came to Master Bodhidharma, who travelled far to this land of the East; after six transmissions it reached Caoxi, and below him Nanyue and Qingyuan divided it into the Five Houses. From the Liang and Tang down to the Song and Yuan, some eighteen hundred men were born into the world as heroes: they counted the dusty world and its carriages and caps as dross, and thought so little of the rank of minister and general that they would not take it up; they took refuge in the Dharma gate, and beneath a single word awakened to their own mind, so that the root of deluded passion that had bound them through kalpas of birth and death was cut off on the spot. Such men were rightly named patriarchs. Were they not resolute great men indeed? Alas, in this latter age we are far removed from the Buddha's time and so have no share in that gracious assembly on Vulture Peak, while the patriarchs of this land, when they appeared in the world, we could not draw near and enter their inner chamber. So we sink into delusion and to this day have not turned back; how sad it is. I have long heard that the imperial palace preserves portraits of the patriarchs of every age, and that the gentleman-recluse Ding Yunpeng of Xin'an painted with a subtlety that yields nothing to Sengyou or Daozi. He happened to obtain the palace draft of eighty-eight figures. Chan Master Daguan had him paint four sets: one was placed at Mount Emei in Shu, one in the patriarch hall at Jinling, one at Mount Kuang in the Five Teats, and one at Nanyue. The layman Jin Jian of the Ministry of Rites asked for one and brought it back east of the lake. Commissioner Wu Shengbai, who was in charge of military observation, came one day to visit and rejoice in it; seeing it, he sighed and said, This is truly a banner of light. Now there was a portrait painter of Jingmen named Shi Cai who excelled at likenesses, so he was told to make a copy. I have observed privately that the commissioner's bearing is lofty and far-reaching, with the air of one who lightly steps beyond the dust; hence his reverence before these likenesses. He too must have drawn near and entered the inner chamber in former lives. Long ago, when Pei Xiu saw the true likenesses of the eminent monks on a wall, he asked Huangbo, The true likeness can be seen, but where is the eminent monk? Huangbo called, Pei Xiu! Xiu answered, and in spite of himself was startled into awakening. I think the commissioner has long planted deep roots of prajñā, and that his awakening of mind is not behind Chancellor Pei. Therefore I have gathered brief lives of the patriarchs and composed a praise for each, to present to him, that they may serve as a family transmission of the mind-seal.
Inscription on What I Wrote of Chan Master Foxin Cai's Protocol for Sitting in Meditation

Whenever I teach people how to practice, I say only this: let go of deluded thoughts; cast off the root of passion; do not follow the mind that arises and perishes. Then through the twelve double hours, whenever you meet circumstances and encounter conditions, at the crucial points of adversity and compliance, when the habitual poisons of love and hate, greed and anger rise up, in that very instant turn a single thought of the light back upon itself and take a clear look, and never let it screen you or carry you away. Bite down hard on it, as though biting an iron nail; then you may be said to have a diamond mind, and to be called a man of ruthless resolve. This is the skill of a Chan practitioner. Like a strongman boxing, he guards every part of his body, left and right, and lets not one drop leak away. Only thus can one be said to know how to use the mind, and to be a bold and nimble patch-robed monk. This old man in ordinary life used just this one piece of talk to instruct people; he was like one selling flat-topped caps at the crossroads. For decades he rose early and slept late to no purpose, and never earned a single coin to buy cold rice with. Looking at it today, he is not to be compared with old Foxin, who spoke of the protocol for sitting in meditation; that is much more like a top scholar teaching children their primer of the Great Man and Qiu Yiji. With such work, the fare of the host is not scanty. If you can truly learn it, you need not fear failing to reach the top scholar's place. Looking back at old Hanshan, he is still the same old curio. If you have the will to leave the world, you would do well to set your heart at ease and, following this old man's model, put your whole life into it. Would not this single sheet of paper serve as a tally for smashing the armies of Māra and escaping birth and death? Make haste and inquire; make haste and inquire.
Inscription on the Seven Buddhas' Verses That the Practitioner Baogui Asked Me to Write

These verses of the seven Buddhas are the mind-dharma handed down from buddha to buddha. The whole canon, the seventeen hundred koans, and even all living beings in their daily present circumstances — down to the insects and worms and the gnats that fly — everything that has consciousness flows out from within this. Since the coming of the Buddha-dharma there has been no lack of things seen and heard, yet those who truly know are few. Most only add to their learning and increase their knowledge and views, and not one can set his foot down here. Chan Master Hongjuefan was banished beyond the seas, to a land without Buddha-dharma, and lodged in a ruined temple; on a broken wall he saw a verse of the Buddha Viśvabhu. Fan held it in mind for a long time, and said of himself that though he had studied the Way all his life, only that day had he attained great joy, and had come at last to the ground of rest and ease. From this we see that the Buddha-dharma is truly no great matter; the student's concern does not lie in wide seeing and broad knowledge, which only swell the obstruction of much hearing. Long ago the old man of the valley, Huang Shangu, excelled at large characters; whenever anyone asked him for calligraphy on fine paper, he would always write out this verse and give it to them. This is enough to show that when the ancients gained the true meaning in this matter they had a gate of liberation all their own, which words cannot reach. In the summer of the xinchou year, when I had risen from illness, I sat cross-legged on a rattan couch; Baogui asked me to write out the seven buddhas' verses on this paper. That night I dreamed I was attending a great man who was doing calligraphy. At first I took up the brush and understood it myself, yet with a certain constraint of manner. The man laughed and said to me, Calligraphy does not work that way. Writing began with the tracks of insects and the prints of birds; it was never a matter of deliberately seeking to be fine. In the dream I watched the wonder of his brushwork and the force of his movement, which no ordinary feeling could conceive. On waking I still remembered it dimly, and so, taking up the mood of the moment, I wrote this out — a student of the man in the dream.

When I first began to study the Buddha-dharma, I was told that regarding all dharmas as like a dream or an illusion is the first wondrous key to entering the Way. Sitting dry in the mountain forests, for thirty years I have never parted from this one thought. Now, looking at this scroll, it is as though it were a matter in a dream. If one seals the mind with this, then all dharmas are so. Extending the same reasoning, reflections in water, images in a mirror, flowers in the sky, heat-hazes — every kind of state is, each and every one, a gate of liberation. Alas, people of the dusty world, wishing with a mind that still thinks, with impure views, to enter the wondrous gate of all dharmas — that is hard indeed. Having no ground of enjoyment in themselves, how can they make others rejoice? Those who later look at this scroll, if they can contemplate it in this way, may enter not only calligraphy but the Buddha-dharma. Baogui mounted the scroll and, seeing that there was still room at the end, asked me again for a postscript.

I have always said that these seven verses are the mind-seal transmitted from buddhas to patriarchs. I am very fond of writing them out and giving them in every quarter — not fewer than several hundred sheets by now. Often I add my own colophon to them, to show that they are the crux of the Chan gate. But I did not know the source of their translation. Now, in the Record of Dharma Protectors, I have found this colophon by Lord Song, which is enough to serve as an authority for the Chan gate through a thousand ages. Therefore I write it out together with the verses, to make it clear to those who practice Chan these days and harbor the pride of superiority without drawing near to the purport of the teachings. Let it be a mirror of Qin.
Colophon on the Four Poems of Grand Adviser Ding Youwu Crossed the Sea

I have heard the ancients say: that a rhinoceros or a tiger cannot shake his spirit is the courage of the hunter; that a dragon cannot alter his countenance is the courage of the fisherman; that birth and death bring no change in himself is the courage of the man of understanding. Birth and death bring no change in him — how much less the mere ends of profit and harm! All who know him within the seas praise Ding Youwu for his iron heart, his upright ardor, and his great talents and broad strategy. I observe that when Youwu, after a hundred reverses, was cast away on the edge of the sea, his face showed no shame whatever; and when he went to the garrison at Guanghai and crossed the cliff gate, the wind and waves rose violently, the mast snapped and the sail flew, and disaster followed disaster, while those beside him wrung their hands in helplessness — the commissioner was leaning on the gunwale singing a poem. The lads all cried out together, The boat is capsizing! The commissioner said, Wait a little, wait a little; let me finish my poem. In a moment the four poems were just finished, and the boat grounded on the sand, and so was not capsized. Then the commissioner laughed aloud and said, You lads nearly spoiled your master's poem. Ah, how could such a thing be reached by iron heart and upright ardor, by great talents and broad strategy alone? There is something greater than these. Meeting it in sudden accident, the original substance shows itself of itself. In the commissioner's daily rest and repose, he does not even know that he is at ease. Hence it is said, To create fitness falls short of laughing; to offer laughter falls short of arranging. Is this not what it means? Therefore I had this poem carved for the commissioner at Haizhu, and wrote these lines after it.
Inscription After Writing the Seven Buddhas' Verses for Youwu

The seven buddhas' verses are the mind-seal conferred and received by the buddhas and patriarchs from of old. For the ancients who awakened to this, they were like a great mass of fire: all birth and death, calamity and trouble, the dust of passion, were scorched away, and could not be touched. Such a one is called a bold and mighty great man, one who grasps the blade of prajñā and holds the flame of the vajra. The layman Youwu is so by nature; has he not practiced this gate through many lives? During the days of shared hardship and marching, we sported together morning and evening, taking the Dharma as our delight. He happened to ask for calligraphy, and so I wrote this to portray his true colors.
Colophon on Copying the Heart Sutra with the Inkstone That Belonged to Lord Bao

I once heard it said that when Lord Bao governed Duanzhou he left not one inkstone behind, and I took it for idle talk. When I came to Guangdong I asked the elders there. They said: Long ago, when Lord Bao governed Duanzhou, he abolished the abuses connected with the costly inkstones of Duan. He happened to obtain a fine one and carried it home with him; as he passed the mouth of the Lingyang Gorge a great wind and wave arose. Lord Bao said, In all my life I have done nothing of which my heart is ashamed, and have had no policy that oppressed the people; why should this be? Then he looked at the inkstone and said, Can it be that the spirit of the mountain grudges me this thing? So he threw it into the water, and the wind and wave subsided. Afterwards, from time to time, a strange light shone upon the water, and a fisherman netted the stone; from then on the strange light was seen no more. Master Luo brought this inkstone to me; I stroked and handled it for a long while, then rejoiced and sighed, saying: Divine things conceal and reveal themselves, each in its own time, and that one should meet with connoisseurship is no accident either. It is said that perfect sincerity can pierce metal and stone. Look at this stubborn rock: Lord Bao's heart-light could blaze forth in it — how much more in that which prajñā has perfumed! Well may it endure through a thousand kalpas and not decay. So, having tried the ink, I wrote out one scroll of the Heart Sutra and gave it to Master Luo.
Inscription on Dongpo's Praise of Avalokiteśvara

Caoxi said, Buddha-nature is impermanent. Zibai, in his colophon to Dongpo's praise of Avalokiteśvara, also said, Suffering and joy are impermanent. Yet suffering and joy are transformations of Buddha-nature, and sage and ordinary being are the gatherings of suffering and joy. If Buddha-nature has a receiver, then suffering and joy belong to it; if it has no receiver, then sage and ordinary being alike vanish. Thus Buddha-nature manifests with suffering and joy; therefore in the suffering and joy of living beings it is the receiverless that receives them. Then one knows that the knower of suffering and joy is that which suffering and joy never reach. When living beings suffer and cry out with the receiverless, the receiverless answers them, like a hollow valley echoing a sound. If a person meets suffering with the receiverless, then it is like hot water melting ice: in that thought it transforms into supreme awareness — what need of any other power? So receiving has the receiverless as its mother, and birth has the unborn as its lord. If those who value birth knew what to value, they would transcend suffering and joy, and birth itself would become superfluous.
Inscription on the Scroll of the Mother of Demons

I look upon the Mother of Demons and see a delusion beyond compare: she knows only to covet what belongs to others and never looks to herself; of what is her own she will not let go a thread; yet toward others she has no compassion at all. All mothers and children are of one substance; could she but see them as equal, her deluded heart would soon be still. Had the Tathāgata not pulled out the root of her delusion, she would have sunk into the depths even to the end of kalpas. Though she had spirit-powers, they all came out of anger and delusion; only where these cannot be used does she come to know herself. When the power of love is at its utmost, the deluded heart is suddenly still; the boiling caldron and the furnace coals are quenched on the spot.
Colophon on the Song of the Great Snow on New Year's Day

In former days I lived with Master Chekong of Huanglong Pool at the Dragon Gate before Yedou Peak in Wutai. One winter the snow fell heavily; the wind rolled it up and buried the huts more than ten feet deep. We sat wrapped in our robes facing one another, feeling only that the night was long. When we rose and opened the door, the snow blocked us in. We hurried to stir up the fire and fetch a lamp, and looked at each other and laughed, taking it that we were buried alive. Presently the master of the North Terrace heard of it and came to the rescue, bringing several dozen novices with tools and dry rations; they dug a tunnel and entered, and when we met inside the joy was warm and full, as though we were beneath the Yellow Springs. Since the day I was banished beyond the mountains, in twenty years, whenever I think of it, what at once breaks this scorching heat is this one thought of a heart of ice. Lately I have passed my old age at Mount Kuang, and first found Master Hanzong Jue, who pointed out the Five Teats for me to dwell in. He is the true-boned descendant of Master Che, and he looks on me as his own master. Each time I see him, I feel as though I were facing Master Che in that snow pit. In the first year of Tianqi, on New Year's Day, three feet of snow fell and ten thousand mountains froze together, no less than in that pit. In more than thirty years since I left Wutai I have not seen such a scene, and so I was moved to make this song for it, and wrote it out for Jue, not forgetting the days when Master Che and I shared life and death. Now Jue carries on the house of Huanglong; if he can embody all that lies before him, knowing that it all came from his master's endurance of cold and hunger, then what feverish affliction will not become cool, and what work of the Way will not be accomplished? There is a proverb: To found an enterprise is not hard; to keep it is hard. If you know the old master's field and weed and hoe it at all times, so that it does not go to waste, then you will know that our original teacher, the monk Śākyamuni, for a hundred thousand kalpas gave up body, life, and wealth, and endured six years of cold and hunger in the Snow Mountains, and so won the four offerings and left them to his sons and grandsons. Every grain of rice and every stalk of vegetable that we eat in daily use is a drop of blood from every pore of our original teacher's body. Reflecting on this, can you still be content to pass this life in vain? But that writing a snow poem should lead me to this is much like catching sight of the great ocean's waves by way of a fisherman. Let the master keep it in mind. Written on the first day of spring of the first year of Tianqi.
Inscription After the Poems on Military Service

Leiyang lies due south of the pole; Dongpo inscribed it, First among ten thousand mountains, and it is what is called the place where the waters end and the mountains run out. Physiognomists call it the exhausted dragon; hence in ancient times loyal ministers and righteous knights who were banished were mostly sent here — the climate made it so. Lord Kou lived here only a short while, yet to this day the elders speak of it with relish. Long ago Dongpo was banished to Dan'er and Ziyou was moved there too; hence the relics of West Lake, Lord Kou's shrine, and Lord Su's pavilion. The excellence of the mountains and streams and the scenes remain as before. Yet of monks who came here to garrison, in the past there was the Song dynasty's Dahui, exiled to Meiyang, and Juefan, sent to Zhuya. Ah, those two elders left me five hundred years ago. Now I too have received grace and been sent here — surely a strange matter spanning a thousand years above and below. In our sage dynasty, the only monk sent to garrison was my first ancestor, Chan Master Nan Zhou Qia, who was punished for shielding the Jianwen emperor; the Chengzu emperor pardoned him, and his disciple Delu was garrisoned here in his place, and soon released. That is two hundred years ago and more. Lately I too, having prayed for the dynasty's welfare, was punished and sent here. Surely this is not without meaning. When I arrived I lodged in an old temple west of the city. In Lord Su's pavilion the scholars vie in talking of Lord Su as though it were yesterday; but when I sought the old story of Juefan, it was utterly gone. The sights of the far south are wholly unlike the central lands, and the qi of the four seasons does not accord with heaven and earth: as when Qian, pure yang, changes into Li, and Li is the direction of fire, where all things appear to one another, thick with heat and spreading as civilization. People see only the thickness of the sights and do not see the wonder of the free flow; hence in letters and verse they cannot exhaust the subtlety of creation. When I first arrived I met a year of pestilence, and so in the midst of it I wrote my commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra, claiming to have peered deeply into the mysteries of buddhas and patriarchs — and truly I had aid from this place. I never sought skill in poetry; but since coming here with the army, my poems have spread through the land, and the wise all regard them as Chan. This is enough to prove that mind and circumstance have melted into one, so that one does not know how it comes about. From this too I know that the wonder of the ancients' poetry lies simply in true feeling and real circumstance. Lord Zi Yuan brought out an album and asked me to write on it. I have written this idly, fit only to cover a jar, and to draw a laugh.
Inscription After the Twelve Poems Written in Illness

That monks have gone to war has happened before. Thus Chan Master Dahui was sent to garrison Meiyang, where he wore the cap and robe of a layman and taught the Dharma; and the Venerable Jiyin was banished to Yazhou, where he wrote his commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sutra. These two elders, by the samādhi of illusion, dwelt in hardship as in play. When I was young and driving off crows and jackdaws, I already knew of these matters and pictured the men. Little did I think that at the age of fifty I too would meet this calamity and, by grace, be banished to Leiyang — a place that lies between those two elders' lands. I am ashamed that I am not their equal, yet I constantly ponder their noble bearing. When I first reached the garrison I at once wrote my commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra; there was something that moved me to it. Whether the times and circumstances I dwell in compare with theirs, I cannot say. But cherishing the Body of Wisdom of the monk and the Dharma as my concern, I hold to one thought and never forget it in my diligence. I would not presume to look to those two elders' walls in Chan and the Buddha-dharma; yet as for firmly upholding the Dharma gate with a lone and steadfast loyalty, I truly have the resolve to gnaw snow and swallow felt. And my longing for the mountains and forests, my old self, takes form in sound and verse — truly a letter tied to a wild goose's foot. In a thousand ages to come, will those who read these poems and picture me picture me as I picture those two elders? Alas, I am old. I write this and give it to my attendant Guangyi, who may keep it as a family model.
Colophon on the Six Chants

The essential purport of the Buddha-dharma does not go beyond the one mind. Because this mind is deluded, there is the suffering of impermanence. Since suffering is fundamentally impermanent, its nature is of itself empty; being empty, I am originally without self; without self, who is it that undergoes birth and death? The whole canon is the mind-seal transmitted by buddhas and patriarchs, and it does not go beyond these six dharmas; in sum, they are not apart from the one mind. If this mind is deluded, there is the suffering of birth, death, and impermanence; if this mind is awakened, then there is no self; without self, one penetrates the emptiness of nature; nature being empty, birth and death are empty too. There is no other wondrous dharma apart from this mind that could be true emptiness. In the past many who set their will on Chan looked for mysteries outside the mind and sought the true teaching outside the world, and so in daily use they missed boundless wondrous practice, supposing that the Buddha-dharma lay elsewhere. They did not know that in our ordinary daily life, responding to conditions and doing our work, all of it is true Buddha-dharma. Only because of the difference between having a self and having no self is suffering and joy not the same, and sage and ordinary being also differ; it all lies in the single interval between delusion and awakening. For the self is the root of all suffering. The magistrate asked for Chan words in my hand, so I have recorded my old Six Chants and noted the matter again, to serve as a tally for attesting this Dharma gate on some future day.
After the Poems Written to Express My Feelings for Lord Li

The ten poems above were written in the middle of the long-day month of the yisi year; the next year, the first month of winter of the bingwu year, I was at Caoxi. I rejoiced to rebuild the patriarch's court, and it was suddenly made new. The meditation hall was the place where the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch, preached, and where the great patriarchs of Nanyue and Qingyuan dwelt in peace; with the changes of the generations it had turned into a rat's nest and a fox's den. Now I have striven to restore the old pattern, and its scale and breadth yield nothing to former days. As for its management and the help given, it was the layman Lin Canjun, Zhizu, who bore it on his single shoulder. I reflected that in former days in the East Sea, when the adorned and wondrously fair Dharma-work was about to flourish, I met with calamity and was exiled beyond the mountains. Who would have thought that I should again conjure up this way-place, to open a conjured assembly, do the conjured Buddha-work, and save conjured living beings? And all the more since I received the gracious decree, the net of Tang thrown wide open: what was bound at the first is freed at the last. One period comes full circle, equal and without two. What is called entering samādhi in the east and rising in the west, entering right samādhi in a monk's body and rising from samādhi in a layman's body — is this not the samādhi of the square net? I cannot forget Lord Li the Censor's first thought of joy, and so I have written out the poems of my feelings for Lord Li and given them to the layman. By this you may see that this humble one is not overthrown by danger and hardship, not moved by circumstances, not affected by different forms and different spheres, not troubled by going or staying, not shaken by evil māras. Who but one who sits on the ground of patience and sits in the field of extinction could easily reach this? The opportunity within this is again the old man's secret family transmission, by no means to be described in words. Can the layman attain it?
Colophon on the Ten Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains (these poems were written ten days before his passing, and are his last writing)

These poems were written at the Five Teats in Mount Kuang, on a spring day of the renzi year. My attendant Shenguang had asked me to write them on this scroll at the time; but the old man was lazy with brush and inkstone, and so it was bundled away on a high shelf. When I returned to Caoxi, on the eve of departure I gave it into the keeping of my attendant Guangsheng to carry with him, and it was stored away a long time. In the ninth month of autumn of the guihai year, Guang came with a letter to visit me; for he had urged Sheng to complete it, but had not. At the time the old man was suffering pain in his feet when he moved, and was wearied by answering questions; Sheng seized the interval to ask again and again. The old man then thought that he was old, and feared to leave a debt for the future, so with effort he forced himself to write despite his illness and send it back. Truly this is sparing two eyebrows for love of a three-year-old child; is it not a grandmother's heart? If one looks only at the poetry and the calligraphy, then one is greatly indebted. Written on the first day of the tenth month of winter of the guihai year.
Colophon on Old Man Zibai's Verses on Contemplating Illness

Old Man Zibai was accustomed to show people the meaning of no-nature; like the hand of one juggling balls, it left every onlooker astonished and dazzled. Since the great elders Xueyan and Zhongfeng, this pointing has rarely been understood. How regrettable that the Way ran counter to the times, and his wish to rouse it was not fulfilled. This was the lifelong bitterness of this old man. Alas, the wise man has gone; how can the young and the latecomers ever see again the standard of the Chan gate? The monk Haimo of Mount Emei brought me these verses on contemplating illness. Seeing them, I could not keep several lines of tears from falling. His written trace is as it was; treasure it as a seed of light.
After the Essay on Fan Li

This essay I wrote in the autumn of the jiyou year, when my boat was moored on the bank of the Pearl River and Canjun Li asked me for a praise on the picture of Fan Li Returning to the Lake; I was moved by it and so composed it. I have often said that when the literati of old judged the men of old, works like those of the three Su are brilliant, yet by and large they never come to this. How is that? So one knows that to seek a kindred spirit a thousand years later is what the ancients found hard, and to hope for a meeting within a single day is no accident. Fan Li's heart is indeed hard to see; that I have brought it out in words means Fan Li too may close his eyes in peace. What is there of past and present, of going and coming? I say that when a great man lives in the world and holds a view that transcends the world, he will surely not easily be known by the world. Hence with dragons and unicorns, every three-foot child in the world knows they are divine and auspicious — but that is because they are not seen, and so people vie in praising them. Should a dragon appear by day, people would take it for a snake; and when a unicorn comes forth, it is sure to be harmed by the gamekeeper. What wonder is there in that? In the ten years I dwelt at Caoxi I was indeed once a dragon and once a snake; only I could not escape one calamity. At the time there was a siege by the men of Kuang that lasted twenty days, in the season of cold dew and falling frost of the jiyou year. On a clear night, when the mood came upon me, my attendant happened to find this blank scroll in a box. I took up the brush in high spirits; the essay lay just then on my desk, and so I wrote it out and noted its meaning thus.
Inscription After the Song on Copying the Lotus Sutra

From my youth I knew how to chant this song; one may say I had entered deeply into the samādhi of the Lotus. Each time I unroll it, I feel my spirit leap and boundless joy arise. I have often written it out and given it to those who seek the Way. Lately I came to Caoxi to set the Sixth Patriarch's way-place in order, and have been at it nearly ten years, working forgetful of myself, so that a hundred neglected things were taken up and the mountain gate took on a new look. Then, unexpectedly, a demonic monk within worked obstruction, ruining the Dharma gate himself, turning things upside down in wild confusion and bringing lawsuits in the government offices, so that I ended up lodging in the prefectural city for two idle years. At that time, of those in the city who took refuge and protected the Dharma, there was only the layman Huang, one day out of two years, morning and evening without interruption, in bitter cold and steamy heat, never failing by a hair's breadth. I was moved to think of how in former days, when Chan Master Juefan was exiled overseas, his close friends and acquaintances scattered like startled birds and fishes, and only Hu Qiangzhong alone attended him and saw him off to Shaoyang; the master wrote a preface to take leave of him. Even now, reading his words, one pictures the man. Now I, a man in exile and hardship, am alone in a field of defilement and right and wrong, and there is a layman to be my wooden tongue, so that the business of the public court is clear as the sun and moon held up. How could this affinity be shallow? Now that the affair is concluded and I am about to set out, I have written out for him a copy of the Song on Hearing and Chanting the Lotus Sutra, to have him recite and study it, so as to form a bond of Dharma-joy. And let this paper be handed down to his sons and grandsons, that later generations may know that their grandfather could knot brows with old man Hanshan, and that by this root of goodness blessing may reach his children and grandchildren and be enjoyed age after age. One may say that this good meeting has not been in vain. Therefore I note it as well.

When I was banished beyond the mountains, my kin and friends fell away from me as though we were separated by the heavens. In the summer of the jiyou year of Wanli, the elder Yitian Xiao of the Cishan Temple in the capital came specially to console me beneath the pines of Caoxi. At the first meeting grief and joy mingled, as though we were men of different worlds. I remembered how in former days, when I begged for food in Chang'an, I had passed through the elder's Xuanming Chamber and washed away the dust of a guest. Now, in this burning wilderness and house of fire, each time I think of it I enter at once a place of coolness. In this dust and filth, to seek a drop of water to wash body and mind — how hard it is to get! In early autumn I had business in Duanzhou, and so I drew the elder along with me. We climbed Precious Moon Terrace and took the cool for ten days or a month, then went on to Wuyang, ate fresh longans, and came home replete. Truly it was a joy. As the boat went north and we pushed upstream with difficulty, the elder brought out this scroll and asked for my writing, so I wrote out this song. The elder said as he went back, I shall have my disciples, one and all, be like the monk on the Panshi Rock, chanting the White Lotus Sutra as their constant daily lesson. Thus they will not only be worthy of Xiunya; then the old man, eight thousand li away, will still be as though beneath the moonlit pines, listening with tilted ear to their chanting.
Inscription on the Thousand-Character Text Written by Master Xuelang En

My elder brother Xuelang En and I were as if born of the same womb: in youth we shared brush and inkstone. I was lazy and often ill, and secretly admired dry Chan; my brother set his will hard on learning, and not only applied himself to the teachings but roamed in the garden of the arts, inquiring widely and remembering much, tireless in eating and resting, dyeing his brush and facing the pool day and night for more than twenty years. When he ascended the seat to teach, he far surpassed earlier worthies, and in letters and writing he held the field, so that he too was called one of a pair of wonders. In two hundred years of our Ming dynasty, the steeds among the black-robed are not to be numbered on a second hand. This is the man I admired and served all my life. I am ashamed that my blessings are light and my karma heavy, so that to old age we were parted; and it is a grief that in his sixtieth year he passed into eternity. Alas, I have lived on to seventy with nothing to repay the Dharma gate; what use is this stolen life? I dwelt in retirement at Nanyue, and had not the monk Feishi brought this scroll, I should not have seen it; seeing it, I could not keep from sorrow, and sighed again and again. Alas, the man is gone, but the written trace is as if alive; looking at it is like meeting Jiguang face to face.
Inscription After the Account in the Bicheng of the Layman Gu Baochuang

The record says: The layman Gu Baochuang of Jinling, whose personal name was Yuan and whose style was Qingpu, was in youth bold and uncommon; in poetry, calligraphy, and painting he did not cling to ancient models, but dotted and dyed with a trusting brush, his natural zest utterly beyond the common — and yet in truth it all came out of the ancient methods. One day he discussed calligraphy with me, saying, In calligraphy four parts should be ancient method and six parts one's own idea, and then it is wondrous. Otherwise, though every stroke resemble the ancients, in the end it is slavish writing and not worth prizing. In middle age he devoted his mind to Chan and had a great awakening. Yet he never slighted the cultivation of causes because he had grasped the principle. In his later years he formed a Western assembly with famous monks, strict and pure in the precepts, without peer. At the end he sat upright and passed away; the whole house smelled the fragrance of lotuses, which ceased only after three days. The layman had once written out several quatrains in his own hand; I copy them here. Ten cushions, nine worn through; whose dry well is so hard to fill with snow? Now every dharma has become samādhi; sights and sounds may reach the ear unharmed. Pine-fire cooks the gruel, fragrance fills the robe; in snowy cold the bold knight has hungered since of old. A bright pearl I would not exchange for a jar of yellow pickles; spittle and spume gleam brighter than sun and moon. Who is it that bustles night and day over tripods of food? The whole mechanism is everywhere, good to examine closely. The fishing rod does not fail the autumn, brocade-bright; on both banks yellow blossoms strike fragrance against the table. In short hempen coat and long hoe I grow old at the stone gate; a plate of greens sees me easily through from dawn to dusk. A hundred years of wit and cunning ground away to nothing; I am ashamed that men hand down the traces of my powdered ink. On the bowl two knives flash like snowflakes; in youth I once drank the Lu family's Zhu Jia drunk. Before my reckoning could unfold a man's ambition, my head was white at the capital gate, learning to plant melons. In the snow-hut and cold pickles there is the glory of the years; gold measured by the peck is not worth boasting of. If you say merit on bamboo and silk is hard to decay, it too but adds flowers to the eye. Vine leaves and green sedge grow long to fit the body; new chrysanthemum wine brims the gourd with fragrance. If folk of the day would visit the layman Pang, ten thousand trees of cloud-vine guard the thatched hall. I who was once given the prediction go loose-haired; in grass robes I belong to an idle body wherever I am. Ten years of friends and old companions, the dust of toil broken through; incense and fire together repay the spring of the wild temple. In the clouds the green hills, an ancient grove of junipers; branch and bough like a roof screen the frost wind. When a man has the will and casts in his lot, a clay bowl is dimly in his hand. This is what the Jiao family's Bicheng records. In my childhood I heard that the layman Gu Baochuang, when he was first a government student, was very bold in temper and quick in talent. In middle age, one day, he cast off all he had practiced and kept a long fast before an embroidered Buddha, building a small tower and sitting alone in it, with only a young boy to bring incense, flowers, and pure water; the women of the household never saw his face, and acquaintances were cut off from all dealings, so that he was a mountain hermit in the midst of the world. Every night at the fifth watch he struck a great wooden fish and chanted the Buddha's name aloud. The layman's house was near the market, where there were many butchers; there was one vicious youth who rose to slaughter as soon as he heard the fish, and one day, being late, he scolded his wife. She said, The man of the Way is striking his wooden fish and chanting the Buddha's name. You hear it and go on killing living creatures, and do not awaken yourself — and you scold me? The youth at once broke his knife and staff and turned his heart to goodness, and for a time many butchers turned their hearts likewise. The gentleman said, I hold my wooden fish and strike it all night long; how many sleepers in dreams have I startled awake? At nineteen I left home under the old patriarch of Xilin at Changgan. The late Master Yungu was the Dharma eye of the age; he lived at Qixia and was especially close to the layman — he is the famous monk of whom the Bicheng speaks. The master told me of this matter and asked what sort of man the layman was. The master said, He is the Pang of our day. One day, strolling idly with companions in the pine garden, I saw a man of the Way enter the mountain gate, of clear and ancient countenance and most refined, at ease like a lone crane soaring in the sky, aloof beyond the dust. Drawing nearer to look, I saw that his eyes did not blink, as though he had no concern for the human world. I was startled and delighted, and said, Who is this man, and why is he so fair? One who knew said, This is the layman Baochuang. I wished to bow to him but was afraid, and so followed to see where he went; I saw him enter the side door of the temple's cloister and bow before the Tathāgata's relic stupa. I watched him secretly: his five limbs were raised in diligence, and his reverence and prostration were beyond words. And I looked at the stupa hall, towering into the clouds, its five colors fresh and bright, its reflected light shining back, red as a jewelled inlay. Suddenly I awakened to this state: surely it was not of the human world. Yet I still did not know why it was so. Afterwards I asked the late Master Yungu, and the master said, This layman contemplates this as the realm of the Western Pure Land, to aid his contemplative practice. From then on, through the master, I was able to enter his inner chamber. At the end, when he was about to die, he and the master, with several famous monks, chanted the Buddha's name face to face for several days and nights, hanging a picture of the Western realm in the room. I was among the assembly, just then doing the Buddha-work, when the layman's wife announced, The whole house smells the fragrance of lotuses. All were startled and delighted; the layman alone was calm and showed no change. What the Bicheng records I saw with my own eyes. The layman's sons were all government students and had never believed in the Buddha. At this they wept before the bed and knocked their heads, asking, Father, if you are to transcend birth and death and dwell in the Pure Land, will you not think of your sons and grandsons and save them too? Why do you leave no single word of instruction? The layman laughed and said, Do you think I am being born, or dying? And have you never looked at the sun? The sun rises in the east and sets in the west: is it really setting, or really not setting? My birth and death are just like this. He took up the brush, wrote this, threw down the brush, and passed away sitting upright. What I saw with my own eyes the Bicheng does not reach so far. One day, idly opening the Bicheng's pages, I came on this episode and was moved to write it out again, and to tell it to those who understand words.
Inscription on the Layman Nangao's Copy of the Scroll of the One Dharma to Which All Dharmas Return

The buddhas and patriarchs from of old have never had a real dharma to give to people; they only strike one blow into the dream of living beings' deluded thought, so that with a shout the dream suddenly breaks and the two eyes open wide, and looking back at the states within the dream, nothing at all can be found. But to set the mind to work on that which cannot be found is also a matter of dreams. From this we see: is there any single dharma that can be taken as an object of feeling? Therefore it is said, Not to see a single dharma is the Tathāgata; this is what is called Contemplating the Sovereign. Hence it is said, Apart from marks and apart from names, one does not fall among the reckonings. If you call it one, then you fall and fall again. The layman Nangao has silently matched this Way and dwells in ease and freedom, and that for some years now. Thinking earnestly how few are those who truly understand the tune, he especially takes up this old koan and often raises it to show people, wishing each to know his own place of falling. If the onlooker takes it up quickly before the layman has raised it, he is still only halfway. If instead he huddles over the one dharma and all dharmas, he is much like a fool being told of a dream. The master Hui'an has long studied under the layman, entering his abbot's room from time to time and hearing the teaching of the gate of non-duality, so that he is already familiar with it. Now tell me: this koan, and Vimalakīrti's silence — are they the same or different? Inquire.
Inscription on the Praises of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra

Lord Zou the Hanlin Academician taught the learning of Yangming for generations, and his son Ziyin inherited the family's mantle. In the spring of the guichou year he visited me at the Green Gate in Wuyang and asked about the meaning of the coming from the West. I had him thoroughly set aside the habitual knowledge and views in his breast and sit in silence for seven days, and then I gave him the medicine. As soon as Ziyin heard it, he at once matched the purport that words cannot express, and was convinced that he had previously fallen into the gateway of light and shadow; he leapt up and went home. When I was at Nanyue, a letter came from his elder brother Ziyin, earnestly declaring that Ziyin had awakened and was freed. Not long after, alas, he passed away. I grieved in my heart for a long time. When I retired in old age to Mount Kuang, nine years later, in the winter of the xinyou year, his son Yuhou sent me a copy of the praises of the Perfect Enlightenment that he had written. Reading it, I knew that though Ziyin had long departed, he had truly never left the great treasury of light; one may say he had deeply planted the right cause of prajñā. Had Heaven granted him years, the height he might have reached could not be measured. How lamentable!
Inscription After the Stupa Inscription of Master Huanyu Ben

Master Huanyu Ben first studied under my own teacher, the monk Yungu, and was born of the same strip as I. In the xinsi year we met at Wutai. I saw his countenance of the Way, clear and lean, too weak to bear his robe, and his mind like the great earth, with the strength to bear living beings; hence he could forget himself for others, and never held the mark of a self for a single thought. That he doctored sick monks so well as to cut flesh from his own body for a remedy tells enough. I was sitting amid ice and snow; one day I was frozen and starving to death, and the master hurried to save me and bring me back to life. I praised him then as a king of physicians. Since we parted more than thirty years have passed, and he entered extinction twenty-three years ago. Formerly, because of the carving of the canon, his relics were kept at the Jizhao Temple at Shuangjing. In the winter of the bingchen year I came on account of the entering of the stupa of Master Da, and the master's chief disciple Gao took the same occasion to bury him. Thus I was able to choose a site for the master and lay his bones in the earth. Ah, what a strange matter; was it not a bond from a former life? Reading the layman Dongguan's stupa inscription for the master, I felt as though I were sitting in the Vajra Cave talking with him. So I wrote a poem to mourn him: Who knows of freezing and starving on the cold cliff? After the end, revival came through the master. Today at Five Peaks I peer at the stupa's shadow, as if still facing him in conversation. I think of this mountain as a Dharma cave of the southeast, where the teachers of eighty-eight generations have taught; what bond from former lives had the master, that he could follow after Master Da and at the last come home to rest here? I am ashamed that I was born of the same strip as the master but shall not die of the same strip; how could I win this one handful of earth to cover my dry bones? I wonder in what generation the master will appear in the world again, and what manner of host he will be. If he gains the power of remembering former lives, he will surely see this old withered one, on the last night of the year, trimming the lamp and writing these words.
Inscription for the Reception Hall of the Thousand Buddha Temple at Golden Bamboo Flat, Mount Lu

Mount Lu is the finest of Jiangzuo's scenes; since Master Yuan opened the mountain in the Jin dynasty, and the teaching seats of the patriarchs of Tang and Song, it has stood alone in excellence under heaven. Its shape is like a green lotus on the water, and Golden Bamboo Flat sits right in the heart of the flower. In past days it was wild thicket; recently the Dharma Master Gonggan built a thatched hut and dwelt alone, consoling his shadow on the cold cliff, and his disciple Xu Fangliang served him with bitter effort. Each time he went begging in the prefectural city he would go by day and return by night, traveling in wind and sleeping in dew, enduring every kind of hunger and cold and hardship. In less than ten years he opened the waste and broke the ground and began to build houses; then Master Gan passed away, and Master Lian kept his dying instruction, forgetting himself to carry it on, and thus it became a monastery. For thirty years he shared sweet and bitter with the assembly, sleeping and rising with them; of every grain of rice and every stalk of vegetable he kept nothing for himself, and put himself first in the work. Now he is old, and sits on the long bench, with no private room at all — he has truly gained the ancients' manner of shepherding the assembly. Therefore patch-robed monks from every quarter come and feel at home. Yet the master does not put forward the Buddha-dharma or the Chan Way; he simply regards the Dharma gate with one flavor of equal compassion, and has never used the breath of rice-gruel to drum up support in every quarter or to boast of his own ability. In this he has deeply attained the samādhi of no-self. Hence none who draw near and rejoice in him fail to be moved and transformed in heart. Every year the mouths to be fed number in the thousands; the master is calm and without care, and does not make the four offerings his own anxiety, nor does he appoint a special master of donations. Yet in the monastery there is scarcely one with a little will who does not of himself agree to run about and put forth effort, begging to gather from every quarter, and by this resonance of reputation the yearly reckoning has never been short. In this too he has deeply grasped our Buddha's supreme teaching of following conditions. In this Dharma-ending age, among those who establish places in every quarter, his kind can hardly be found again. The old man has come to rejoice in it and cannot finish his praise; and seeing all the practitioners return from begging without the least confusion in cause and effect, not betraying the donors' faith, and observing closely the practitioners who manage monasteries in other quarters, I find none so true and real as this. This must be the response of dragons and gods to the sincerity of the master's true heart; it is no accident. The old man's gratitude has no end; therefore I write this in general terms, to tell the donors. As for the four offerings and the giving of the seven treasures like Mount Sumeru, these too can be consumed — but there are great-hearted bodhisattvas for that, and the old man would not venture to decide it.
Inscription After the Scroll of Master Zhulin of Mount Tai

In former days the old man dwelt in the golden realm, and there knotted brows with old man Zhulin alone. As I was about to set out, he entrusted me with a dung broom, charging me again and again to be a serving lad in Mañjuśrī's house. Since we parted more than thirty years have passed, and since the old man was moved to the burning wilderness more than twenty years. Though ten thousand li separate us, in every outgoing and incoming breath there has never been the least gap between me and this old man. Now, suddenly seeing this scroll, old man Zhulin's body shines upon the old man's brows. Who says this old man has entered extinction? He does not know that in the samādhi of the square net one enters concentration in the east and rises in the west: entering concentration at Mount Tai, rising at Mount Kuang — this is just this old man's everyday tea and rice. Now tell me: has Zhulin come or not? Best for each of you to sweep the dung as before. Should a student carry this into every place of daily use, let him not defile the broom handle. Only then is it requiting kindness with kindness.
Inscription After the Life of the Wall-Light Boy Shen Dayu

Living beings inherently possess the Buddha-nature, which is called prajñā; it is endowed with a great light that shines constantly and is never dim. It is only because of beginningless ignorance that it is dimmed and unrecognized; and because ignorance is deep and thick, one lies in birth and death forever without knowing it. Therefore when bodhisattvas cultivate, they simply use the light of wisdom to shine through ignorance — that is the time of escaping birth and death. Hence those who cultivate the mind are called students of the practice of prajñā. Those in the world whose wisdom is keen come from prajñā, and when it issues as loyalty and filial piety, it is their nature making it so; and even at death and birth they do not see the marks of coming and going, for the eternal light shines. Look at the boy Shen Dayu: he lived only eight years, and all his words and deeds were the practice of prajñā from former lives, so that at the end his single thought was bright, and the eternal light was undimmed. This prajñā appearing at the very moment of death is enough to show the surpassing strength of prajñā. Ah, seeing this, was he one who falls into birth and death? Yet his parents looked on him with love, which turns prajñā backward into a root of birth and death — would the boy not laugh at that? Through what should have been his salvation he was rather burdened; they have betrayed the boy's purpose in coming. On the sixth day of the third month of the dingji year his father, the layman Erhou, showed me this life, and old man Hanshan inscribed it thus — driving out a wedge with a wedge. When the boy hears of it, he will surely give a laugh.
Inscription After the Diamond Sutra Written in Blood

This sutra was written in blood pricked from her finger by the virtuous lady Zhang, wife of Kang Mengxiu of Huating. The lady was a niece of Lord Wang, the Minister of War, Yuanmei. The lord's elder sister married into the Zhang family and gave birth to the lady, then died young, and Lady Wang the Dowager raised her herself. In childhood a female teacher was engaged to instruct her in the Odes and Documents; she was skilled in brush and ink. She served Kang's mother, and in twenty years of widowhood her reverence and compliance were as on the first day. She was filial by nature; though born in a house of wealth and rank, she was by temperament plain and did not adorn herself with lead and powder. Kang's mother in her old age worshiped the Buddha more earnestly and paid reverence to Master Daguan; the lady practiced vegetarianism and delighted in giving. The Dowager Wang bade the Minister and his brothers look on the lady as their own child; the family estate allotted to her, reckoned in the tens of thousands, she gave all away as a field of blessing, turning her heart to the Pure Land, as if she were one among the lotuses. In her later years she pricked her finger and wrote out one scroll of this sutra in blood; at the end she bade the whole household chant the Buddha's name aloud for days and nights together, and passed away peacefully. When I was banished beyond the mountains, the minister's younger brother Jixiu became my friend outside the world. Lately, when he came to Guangdong, Jixiu sent me a letter asking an inscription for this sutra the lady had written. Looking at the trace of her hand, it is upright, dignified, and finely regular; the brushwork takes the ancients as its model and never neglects a hair, with no trace of softness or warmth. This too is hard for a man to achieve. Stroking the scroll and reading it again and again, I sighed deeply and said: This is the overflow of the light of her mind. Prajñā means wisdom, and it is what all sages and ordinary beings alike are endowed with and share. The buddhas realize it as the diamond mind-ground and manifest it as spiritual wonders; living beings are deluded about it and make of it the root of birth and death, issuing as deluded thought and the toil of dust. The nature is the same but the marks differ. If one would turn the toil of dust and deluded thought into spiritual wonders, it cannot be done without relying on the surpassing power of prajñā. Hence it is said, If there is one who can believe this sutra, he has already planted good roots in the presence of countless millions of buddhas. From this one knows that the lady, dwelling in the world all her life, was like a lotus in the mud, unstained; she firmly believed in the Three Treasures, truly reverenced this sutra, upheld it without doubt. Had she not long practiced prajñā through many lives until it was ripe, how could she have been so diligent? How sad: people in the world all receive the wisdom of spiritual brightness and bear this manly body of flesh and blood, yet give free rein to greed and anger and create boundless dark karma, so that many sink into the bitter paths. Who can sprinkle a drop of blood into the ocean of wisdom and flow along with the Dharma-nature? The Diamond is named for its indestructibility; the prajñā of letters is the eternal abiding of the Dharma-body, blazing with light and shining without end. What is called the diamond seed, unground away through kalpas — how could it be merely a family treasure?
Inscription After Lord Zhu the Hanlin Academician's Appeal for the Restoration of the Baoguo Temple at Nanxun

The ancient Baoguo Temple at Nanxun in Huzhou was first built in the Song dynasty. For more than five hundred years its halls have stood in ruin; monks and laity pass by and do not ask about it, and there is none to call out and lead. A certain novice monk of the temple made a vow to restore it, and swore to cut off one arm to make the assembly's resolve firm. Lord Zhu the Hanlin Academician wrote a piece to spread the matter abroad. The temple's monk brought it past Mount Jing, and I read it over three times and was greatly moved. It is said that the tombs of emperors and kings mostly become mounds of ruin, while Buddhist temples, though decayed, still stand; the Golden Valley and the bronze camels may be taken as examples. The proverb says, A thousand years of fields, eight hundred owners — whose son is able to hold an estate for several hundred years? Or is there a descendant who, like the novice, would make light of the family estate by cutting off a limb? The sutra says that a Buddha-realm is firm, made of diamond, and guarded by dragons and gods; and disciples keep it through the generations. Tracing it to its beginning, it is all the wealth given by the many donors, and so it does not perish through a thousand autumns. Compared with the duration of a family estate, this is clear beyond doubt. Everyone knows that the novice cut off his arm and vowed to raise up the Buddha-realm; but they do not know that the novice's one arm is the imperishable estate kept for the many donors through the generations. A wise and discerning gentleman who can give up impermanent wealth and place it on firm ground will have merit that does not decay for a thousand years to come, and it will be guarded by the novice's one arm — far better than sons and grandsons by ten or a hundred times, and how much more so when the measure of blessing is like space? The lord says that a desolate grave mound endures long thanks to the Buddhist temple; this is truly a Dharma eye. I know that when a man of understanding leads the way, the crowd will rise and respond. Looking at this, the golden temple will be raised at once; it should be like Indra lifting a single blade of grass — this is the novice manifesting a thousand hands and eyes.
Inscription After the Two Stele Texts of the Bronze Hall at Longchang Temple on Mount Hua

My friend Master Miaofeng early entered the Way through the contemplation of the Dharma-realm; hence all that he established in his life flowed out of Samantabhadra's vow and the mind of the Dharma-realm. This is so of his past merit in general, and the matter of the bronze halls makes it clear. For Mount Emei, Mount Putuo, and Mount Wutai are the three great bodhisattvas' sites of bodhi, the most excellent places for benefiting living beings in this land of Zhen Dan; at each he cast a bronze hall to enshrine a venerable image. The one for the southern sea was blocked by circumstances, and so it was placed at Mount Hua in Jinling. Through the loving favor of the sage ancestor, he moved the great compassion of the holy mother and the holy sovereign, who became his donors of gold, and so it took its place alongside the three mountains — a rare affinity indeed. Its adornment and beauty and the breadth of its halls I have not been able to bow before, being carried astray by the power of karma. But the two officials' stele texts, by the Academician Jiao and the Minister Huang — their samādhi of the brush-tip is enough to show a jewelled king's realm appearing at the tip of a single hair. How can one not believe it? Though the three calamities spread abroad, the practice remains serene; held by the power of vows, it will equal the Dharma-realm.
Inscription on the Ullambana Scroll of True Compassion and Perfect Filial Piety

The sutra says, Greatly filial is the venerable Śākyamuni, who through kalpas has repaid his parents' kindness. For all the many lives in which Śākyamuni practiced were grounds for repaying his parents. Hence the Brahmā Net Sutra says, Filial piety is called the precepts: that is, being filial and obedient to father and mother, and indeed to all living beings. Now the precepts are the root of becoming a buddha, and filial piety is again the root of the precepts. So one knows that when buddhas and bodhisattvas save living beings and bring them out of every affliction, it is all the practice of filial compliance. Since living beings through kalpas of birth and death come and go through the six paths, casting off one body and receiving another, there is no kind of being they have not passed through; hence there is no kind that has not been their father or mother. Moreover, only when all living beings are saved does one attain bodhi. Therefore each living being brought out of suffering is the bodhisattva's heart of fulfilling filial piety. How could this be spoken of in terms of a single life or a single body? Even Maudgalyāyana's rescue of his mother of one life does not exhaust the Tathāgata's perfect filial piety. The teaching has the Water and Land Assembly, established to repay parents and to encompass the whole Dharma-realm: all that walks on land, in water, or in air, and even the three woeful paths and the six ways, are wished free from the bitter rounds. Though this belongs to the teaching of images, it unfolds the Tathāgata's root of great filial piety. The monk Lihuan of the capital brought the scroll for the founding of the Ullambana offering and asked for instruction. I inscribed it: True Compassion and Perfect Filial Piety — for the Ullambana extends the meaning of the root of the precepts. Should monks and laity understand this, how could they regard it as mere worldly convention?
Prefatory Note to the Lament for the Officers and Men of Liaoyang

The conjured man, aged and withered, a bundle of bones, hides his shadow in the empty mountains and shuts his door to rest. Just then Lord Tao Xiangru of Yuzhang came to visit; we spoke of the affairs of the day, and he brought out his matching piece to the Academician Zhang's lament for the officers and men of Liaoyang and asked me for a preface. The conjured man read it three times and sighed, saying: Here the spirit of the heroes and loyal knights of old and now is moved beyond the body; this is surely not the common feeling of worldly truth. Hence it is said, The man of will and the man of benevolence do not seek to live at the cost of benevolence; they may kill themselves to complete benevolence. What is benevolence? It is the true nature of this mind, bright and vast, eternally and always so. If one takes the false for the real and loses the true, then one rots with the grass and trees; though alive, one is not alive — what use is it? But if one can hold to the will and forget the body, and with the body forgotten the mind remains, then one will vie in brightness with sun and moon. Thus the loyal ministers and righteous knights of old, when they died for their country, made the country their body; when they died for the world, they made the world their body. Therefore the qi of loyalty and righteousness fills the universe and stands awe-inspiring and undimmed; this is but its proper place. Now, looking at how the two generals died in the place that befitted them, they could rouse the feeling of the men of benevolence and the gentlemen of a whole age. What cannot be snatched away is the will; what cannot be darkened is the mind. What is called seeking benevolence and gaining benevolence: though they die, they can have no regret. Reading the Academician's text, my heart's blood spurted and scattered; the spirit of generous grief and vehement song is bleak and cold as on the Yi River. We shall see heroes rise under this one drumbeat, stirred to righteous bearing, exhausting loyalty and giving their lives to defend the altars of the state — this is what I look for in our day. How could it be merely a piece of writing?
Inscription After the Life of Master Jichuan Chuan, Abbot of Longshu Hermitage

Looking through the heroes of old, those who gave their single body for the urgency of the state and in the end were known to the world for loyalty and righteousness, and called great men — such are rarely seen in any age. And is this true only within the world? Those outside the world have it too. Reading the life of Master Chuan, I was deeply moved. For where a monastery stands is a frontier of the Dharma-realm, and Mount Hua at Wumen is one corner of that frontier. At the time the master was a layman, and he resolutely abandoned wife and children, shaved his head, and became a disciple, giving his body for the Buddha-land; in the end he preserved it whole before departing. Was this not the deed of a great man? And to accomplish the work yet not dwell in it is again what the ancients found hard. It is said, Only because he does not dwell in it is it not taken from him. The master truly has this.
Hanshan Deqing's Dream Wanderings Collection, Scroll 33
Praise of the Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara (with Introduction)

The Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara was Śākyamuni's teacher. In a past age, when a bond existed, they met without intent: because the Bodhisattva spread his hair to cover the mud and offered blue lotuses in worship, he received the prediction and so realized bodhi. Now, beholding the radiant image, I revere and long for it with raised head; burning incense and bowing, I speak this praise.

I bow my head to Dīpaṃkara, the teacher of my teacher. His wondrous working has no limit; therefore I take refuge. The bright sun adorns the sky, and all things are mirrored in it; the full moon in the cold void, and all the stars appear together. It lights what is unlit and shines on what is unshone. Only this lamp of wisdom is bright and blazing. It holds the command of the Dharma king and wears the seal of true reality. Firm as a boulder, utterly at peace, it stills the ten directions. Its mind is like space, and nothing is not contained in it; when one knocks, it resounds like a great bell. Its countenance is utterly still, calm and quietly settled; looking up to it and gazing, all obstructions are at once stilled. Meeting by the convergence of conditions, gaining without intent, with blue-black hair covering the head like a single blue lotus petal. Spreading his hair to cover the mud, with sincere devotion he took refuge; holding flowers in offering, and purity was what he prized. Supreme bodhi he then received as prediction. The dark pearl of the formless image admits no thought or discussion. Mind seals mind, and light melts into light; the Body of Wisdom is measureless, and its merit has no end.
Praise of the Mother of Buddhas on Palm Leaves (with Introduction)

Guangdong is a wellspring of the Dharma-way. Bodhidharma came by sea, and the Sixth Patriarch came forth in answer to the prophecy; Buddhabhadra cut his arm and wrapped the ocean eye, and another master forgot his body and carried the Laṅkāvatāra. All first came forth in the immortal city and first opened the Dharma's course. Since then, for a thousand years, it has been sparse — is it that they came forth there and vanished here, that the ancients alone bore it and those of today have no share? It depends on how one guides them; hence the saying, It is not that there is no Chan, only that there is no teacher. These words have flavor. When I was banished by grace to the mountains and seas, Commissioner Zhou of Haimen, who was in charge of the salt administration, came on his rounds. He is one of the present-day gentry who possesses the true Dharma eye, and he is bound to me by the Dharma; whenever we speak, he makes it his business to show people the supreme meaning. On the thirteenth day of the second month he came with Zha Ruding to the Zhu family's thatched hall, where the sons of the Liu and Wan families were all gathered, and he greatly spread abroad this matter. Each of the sons brought forth the supreme mind of the Way, and the youngest said, Formerly I did not know the Buddha; now I know the mind. Since the mind is the Buddha, I shall make the Buddha my business. The second son asked the gentleman-recluse Jiang Buren of Yue to paint this image. With joy I bowed my head and spoke this praise.

The Buddha's substance is like space, and there is no place it does not contain; walls and tiles, to one who penetrates them, are transparent. Autumn waters are clear and still, morning clouds are bright and glowing; the scene falls into the heart of the wave, and light floats on white silk. To know it is not to see it; to see it is not to know it. It is a flower in a clouded eye, the track of a bird in the vast void. On the palm leaf there is no writing, and the Dharma-body is not a thing. Ten thousand ravines of pine sound make the lion's roar. Blue-eyed and whiskered, the sick-boned Vimalakīrti leaks through the body's frame, yet brows and eyes are clear. A shout! Deep in a hundred flowers the partridge cries; a single note shatters the green of the spring hills.
Praise of the Three Sages of the West

I bow my head to the Lord of Still Light, the Great Master of Measureless Life, who with a mind of extinction can manifest form throughout the ten directions and enter every living body, becoming the lord of birth and death. Like the light of sun and moon, he accomplishes illumination without intent, and none on whom that light shines fails to fulfill their life. Again, like a loving wet nurse who can fathom an infant's mind, giving suck in due measure to hunger and fullness and never letting the milk become a sickness. I see the people of the world: when sick or in pain they always call on the mother, taking the mother as their own mind; if they do not call, they cannot free themselves. Therefore in the three realms, whoever has feeling cannot by himself release suffering and joy; but if he happens to think of my teacher, then by the teacher's compassionate light, which first enters living beings' minds, a single shining in the interval must bring him out of the suffering of birth and death. How much more, since he has great power and has gained great compassion, and compares and transforms beings, so that none is not transformed. Mountains of knives and forests of swords suddenly become jewelled groves; the boiling caldron and the furnace coals become the water of eight virtues. All this is made by one's own mind, transformed within a single thought, like leaven in milk: the ghee is not sought outside. How much less should a forest of thorns fail to become a pure land? Therefore to think of my teacher must be as a child remembers its mother; when child and mother remember each other, there is none who does not meet. When remembrance reaches its utmost, all thoughts cease, body and mind are suddenly void, Still Light appears before one, and illumination and function break forth at once. This very bitter and filthy body then becomes the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Only then does one know that within sun and moon there is nothing that is not Ultimate Bliss.
Praise of the Transformation Buddha

Like a man, yet not a man; sun-faced, moon-faced. Where has he come from? He appears right here. When seen, he is not recognized; when recognized, he is not seen. A flower in a diseased eye, lightning in the vast void. Meeting anyone, each one exclaims in wonder — just look at his single-flavored practice of skillful means.
Praise of the Buddha of Austerities in the Snow Mountains

His heart and liver are ice and frost; his body is earth and wood. Handsome by birth, with a naturally uncommon frame. It is not that he would not give up the palace — only that he did not care to eat meat. He walked into ten thousand folds of cold cliff and endured every desolation and loneliness. One day he grew so hungry that his eyes bloomed, and by mistake he took a bright pearl for a fish's eye. His whole body drew deep into right and wrong, and to this day he harbors grievance. How often has he met people and spoken of his original heart? Just as he would open his mouth, tears streamed down. Tears streamed down. He does not know who is a kindred spirit; could he but meet one, his heart's wish would be fulfilled.

He did not cling to the royal palace, nor stay in Tuṣita. He put off his jewelled and royal robes and buried his body in a thousand fathoms of snow. His thin bones are like firewood, his firm heart like iron. For six years of cold and hunger his mouth could hardly open; again and again he pondered, yet his mind never so much as blinked. One morning he suddenly saw the bright star, and all his former deluded thoughts came to rest. Then he would have pressed into the noisy throng, but his eyes were full of wind and dust and he only stumbled about. Instead he drew the talk of the times, short and long; who knew that cleverness would turn to clumsiness? To this day his grievance is unspoken, and though his whole body is a mouth he cannot explain it. Cease explaining; it is a waste of twists and turns, and he pours out his heart and guts in empty talk. Boundless spring light, a hundred birds crying; the cuckoo cries until the empty hills bleed.

His body fallen into snowbillows, his mind cold as autumn water, inside and out utterly transparent — where then is this or that? To think of it does not reach it; to compare it finds no likeness. Unreachable even in dreams, who can conjecture it? If you would seek it, the points of right and wrong rise in swarms; only do not think, and it is naturally so.

Bones like firewood, mind like snow, thought like ice, face like iron. Had he not been a man of firm heart and fierce hatred of evil, how would he have cast off home and lightly given up his estate? Luckily he had the bright star to change his lot, and so escaped having others laugh and wag their tongues at him.

Worldly thoughts are withered, all conditions utterly cast aside; a thousand-foot cold crag, ten thousand years of ice and snow. When body and mind are laid down at once, all former deluded thoughts come to rest. All come to rest. Just look at a few sparse stars and one wheel of bright moon.

Bones lean, mind cold, ice withered, snow old. If it were not this turning about, in the end it would not be good. Six years of cold and hunger were truly hard to bear; happily the bright star rose early. In the beginning he foolishly loved that little bit, which has made his sons and grandsons lie in the wild grass.

He tossed away the golden wheel-rolling king like spittle he was done with, and buried his body in the Snow Mountains, with not a hair of business left. Sitting upright in bitter reflection, he did not know for whom it was, waiting only for the bright star to rise and give him a blow on the head. How much better than when he had not yet awakened: the bright moon hangs clear on the coral branch.
Praise of the Dharma-body of Vairocana Tathāgata (with Introduction)

I was lodging in the Traveler's Rest Hermitage, expounding the Śūraṅgama Sutra for the white-robed laity, when my disciple Wang Anshun brought a portrait of Vairocana Tathāgata about three feet high, in which the whole body's garment folds and the halo above the head were written all over with one copy of the Avataṃsaka Sutra. The characters were like needle tips and mustard seeds, yet every dot and stroke was distinct; the lines were like drifting gossamer, floating like loose hair. Where the body was at the chest, one foot two inches wide, there were more than two hundred and twenty lines of characters; on the edge of the halo, about two inches around, there were several hundred lines. Its fineness and minuteness exceeded even that of the body, and truly it was beyond thought or discussion. Because the color was old and it could not be read, my attendant looked closely and made out on the left arm the words, In each and every mote of dust, all buddhas. So I knew the sutra was the Flower Garland without doubt. Seeing it, I rejoiced and leapt up and sighed, saying: Had he not been empowered by the Tathāgata's most subtle wisdom, he could never have reached this. Yet how could it be attained by coarse, floating imagination? So I burned incense, bowed my head, and spoke this praise.

I have heard that the buddhas' subtle wisdom is what realizes the wondrous Dharma-body, which is everywhere within living beings' minds and thought, and can perform inconceivable karma. Now I see a living being's subtle wisdom entering everywhere into the Tathāgata's Dharma-body, and within a single subtle pore adorning the inconceivable ocean of Dharma-nature. A single hair, a single mote, is by nature suchness, containing inexhaustible treasuries of merit, like a clean crystal vase filled with fine mustard seeds: all is brilliantly manifest without obstruction, neither broken nor mixed, each in its place. Let one have the keenest eyes of Li Lou and strain his sight to the utmost, he cannot discern it. At first one contemplates the Dharma-body as originally without marks; now one sees the Buddha taking the Dharma as his body. The Dharma-body is originally not apart from living beings, and so it appears from within subtle thought. Thus living beings' minds and the Tathāgata are without two, without difference, each entering the other. Such subtle, pure merit had long fallen into dark and murky obscurity; it is like a mote of dust containing a great sutra, which only an eye of wisdom can see. Excellent, son of the Buddha, whose power of wisdom is bold: one who sees it at once gives rise to true faith, splits the mote of dust and brings forth this sutra, so that I enter at once the ocean of the Flower Treasury. Since the Buddha's mind is just living beings' minds, my entering is the same as living beings' entering. My body, the Buddha, and living beings all mutually enter and contain one another like a net of pearls.
