This perfect great Dharma-realm depends wholly on the son of the Buddha's power of faith to uphold it. With this power of faith he does the Buddha-work and draws and transforms without bound. If one sees and hears, rejoices, bows, or chants in leisure, he can in a snap of the fingers accomplish right awakening. Therefore I praise the son of the Buddha's virtue, vast as space and beyond measure. I vow that all living beings in the Dharma-realm may universally enter the abiding of the son of the Buddha's faith.
Praise of the Contemplating Buddha

I bow my head to my teacher: why does he walk alone? For three times seven days he pondered how beings might be saved. No need to ponder; simply practice equanimity. Should he meet a kindred spirit, that one will of himself awaken sharply.
Praise of the Buddha Beyond Thought and Discussion

Silently contemplating, for whom does he contemplate? The place where he contemplates — who knows it? The ten directions are one thought; living beings are one mind. Whoever knows this is a kindred spirit. The bright moon is in the sky and its reflection appears in all waters: it neither goes out nor enters, and is neither there nor here. Like a cloud floating in the sky, it pervades without intent. At the tip of a single hair the ten directions appear together; all is perfectly accomplished, all conditions complete. Only do not contemplate — then you are the Tathāgata of suchness.
Praise of the Buddha of Measureless Life (with Introduction)

I formerly recited the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations, and took the contemplation of the Buddha as first; hence none who cultivate the pure work fails to apply themselves to it. As for the painters, each has his own model, and in the case of Buddha images it is especially hard, for to manifest a wondrous image in the mirror of a defiled and turbid mind — how could that be easy? Jiang Taiqing of Yue, though young, is uniquely skilled in this art; is it not the fruit of contemplation in a former life? In the second year after I entered Guangdong, in the spring of the wuxu year, Jiang also arrived. The buddhas and bodhisattvas he painted were fewer than ten, and he left to the layman Chen Yuanyu of Lianfu alone the image of the Three Sages, exquisite beyond compare. The layman had kept a long fast before an embroidered Buddha for years, and so perhaps this too came of spiritual resonance. Alas, Jiang soon passed from the world, and the sight of this has become a thing of a thousand ages. The layman burned incense, bowed his head, and asked for a praise. I was carried far in feeling. The praise says:

I bow my head to Measureless Light, shining through the bounds of the ten directions, utterly still and inconceivable, forever breaking the darkness of delusion. I contemplate the realm of extinction, pure and free of the least dust: the great earth and its mountains and rivers — from what place after all do they arise? The mountains of knives and the forests of swords — who made them? It is truly because one's own mind is deluded that firm deluded thoughts congeal, as water becomes ice by the urging of the karmic wind. Within the dream of feeling and perception one undergoes this burning torment. My teacher looks on with cold eyes; his own mind cannot bear the detail, and so he manifests this monk's body and urgently beats the drum smeared with poison, so that all who hear it have birth and death cut off at a single touch. It is like a wondrous lotus rising, spreading lush out of autumn water. Again with the power of great compassion he leads on the left and pulls on the right, until the road of fear is turned into the land of Ultimate Bliss. Where deluded thoughts cease, right awakening appears before one, like hot water melting ice — only by the power of transformation. How wonderful, good man, whose practice of prajñā in former lives was deep, that with the tip of a single hair he can manifest this rare thing. Solemn as at the time of the great vow, diligent and joined in grief and longing, bright as the full moon at peace, roaming in ultimate emptiness. When the defilement of the mind-water clears, image and light appear at once; feverish affliction becomes cool, and all thoughts are suddenly extinguished. The ground of true permanence and wondrous joy is not sought outside; this conjured body then ascends to the Land of Peace and Nurture. Endowed with this inconceivable power — therefore I take refuge. I vow that to the end of the future it may forever be a great reliance.

I bow my head to Measureless Life, who sits upright in the Still Light and shines universally on the emptiness of the Dharma-realm, embracing and receiving living beings. Living beings, deluded about what they originally have, follow arising and ceasing and turn in the six destinies like a lost child who has turned his back on his mother. The kind mother remembers her child and never abandons him for a single thought; if the child but turns the light back for a moment, there is none who does not see her. By my vow to escape suffering I enter the Buddha's mind of embrace, like space meeting space, like water poured into water. Living beings' darkness of ignorance is just the Still Light; when deluded thought ceases for a moment, the eternal light appears on the spot. Arising and ceasing have no coming or going; the Dharma-nature is fundamentally unmoved. Seeing this Dharma-nature body, Measureless Life is forever joyful.
Praise of the Buddha Who Receives and Guides

I bow my head to the Compassionate Honored One, great gathering of bright light, body of the pure Dharma-realm, inconceivable. All suffering living beings enter the eye of great compassion; the eye is pure and dustless, perfectly bright and answering every feeling, entering living beings' minds like the moon falling into water. When the mind-water is clear, there is no this or that. Not receiving yet coming, without birth yet arriving — therefore my teacher forever abides in the world.

He could not bear the cold ground, and so entered the dust with lowered hand, clearly showing himself to people — yet people do not know he is there. Let them but consent to turn the light back for one thought, and the lotus appears at once, with no long delay.

I bow my head to the Lord of Still Light, pure and wondrous Dharma-body, like the moon appearing among the stars, utterly still in all waters. Because he pities living beings, he does not enjoy the bliss of the Dharma-nature but manifests in mote-like lands, bending and lowering his hand of skillful means to lift up those of weak capacity and bring them home together to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Since living beings are the mind itself, that land too is not outside the mind. Only by sealing mind with mind, like pouring water into water, do those who see and hear take refuge in a single thought. Just contemplate your own mind: there is originally no Buddha outside the mind. Form and marks are like flowers in the sky, still seen by a clouded eye. Only with pure emptiness, utterly still and without marks, does one see one's own mind and so see the Suchness.

He sits in the Still Light and rests in the pure land; lowering his hand he enters the marketplace for living beings' sake. With the original Dharma-body he manifests in living beings' minds, and so throughout the ten directions all know his name. By the power of his compassionate vow he universally receives them all; hence those who call his name must attain accomplishment. The nine grades of lotus terraces are the mother of living beings; without borrowing any other condition, he is the host within the guest.

I bow my head to Measureless Light, whose body fills the Dharma-realm, receiving all living beings and bringing them home together to the ocean of extinction. The land is originally neither pure nor defiled; purity and defilement change with the mind. If the mind's defilement is wiped away, the pure realm appears as the thought turns. The Buddha is in living beings' minds, hidden from view by defilement; when the defilement is removed the Buddha appears before them, and there is no need of another to guide them. The Buddha himself saves living beings, and originally there is no mark of this or that. If one can contemplate them equally, that is the land of Still Light.
Praise of the Reclining Buddha
With no business, he lies down to sleep, so happy he could die. Throughout the ten directions, who else can be like this?
Praise of Amitābha Buddha

His mind is like the cold void, his face like the full moon. He sits on a jewelled lotus and puts forth his broad and long tongue; the flowing water and the moving wind ceaselessly proclaim it. The six paths and the four kinds of birth — no capacity is left unembraced. Whoever merely calls his name at once gains liberation. Only because his vow in the beginning was deep, the ten directions are all the land of the unborn.

I bow my head to the Great Master, whose light is measureless, fully endowed with the two adornments, named the honored among the honored. With compassion he gathers in the mind, and his mind embraces worlds as numerous as sands; living beings are the mind itself, originally with nothing outside. Therefore to call his name is to seek oneself. I vow to see my teacher; that is all.
Praise of the Picture of the Long-Fast Embroiderer of Buddhas

His spirit dwells in contemplation of principle and wondrously matches the Dharma-body; his thought clarifies the Pure Land, and in the midst of the worldly he is true. Not dwelling in marks, he is freed from all dust. Thus should one abide and thus subdue one's mind. This is what is called a man of the Way without business.
Praise of Śākyamuni Buddha

I bow my head to my original teacher, whose face is like the full moon, whose pure Dharma-body is utterly still and eternally quiescent. His body is like space, his mind like water; space and water join the sky, and moonlight is like washed silk. The moon does not leave the sky, the water does not leave the earth; space meeting space, above and below without bound. Clouds rise in the long sky, wind moves on the water, waves brim over everywhere — the mark of the broad and long tongue. If you do not believe, then listen to the sound of the tide: it unfolds the secret treasury of the dragon palace.

Only our World-Honored One, wondrous gathering of merit, is like a flower in the sky, responding to the world as conditions come. His Dharma-voice is like thunder, and those who hear it have their hearts broken. Had he not cut away and come from the royal palace, who would do the work that benefits gods and men?

He came from Tuṣita, and not without cause: for one great matter he specially manifested this body. He had hardly left his mother's womb when there was great astonishment; he went off to the Snow Mountains and turned it into a defeat. Happily there was the bright star, and a single cry woke him; had he not turned his head, he would nearly have fallen into a pit. Then he came back among men and leaked a great deal, the root great but the gain slight, nursing vain vexation. At the end he threw it all over and tipped out the whole tray; he met a kindred spirit, and only then wiped away his grievance. A lotus on his tongue, a living matter before his eyes; heart and liver meeting, the void shattered. Therefore the wise deeply know his bitter heart, and so stake body and life and forever turn this sutra.

The light of the Dharma-body is like the shadow of the sun, shining through the world and waking people from their dreams. Bright and dark are one emptiness; sage and ordinary are one awakening. If it does not pierce through to the crown of the head, that is bondage to dharmas.
Praise of the Embroidered Śākyamuni Buddha

I bow my head to the Great Able Sage, savior of living beings, who manifests in this turbid and evil world like a lotus rising from water. His wondrous marks, the thirty-two, are all adorned with merit; hence those who see him rejoice, as when beholding a loving father and mother. Truly he is equal with living beings' minds, without difference; hence from skillful contemplation he appears exactly at the tip of the finger. Living beings' deluded thoughts are threads that weave the forms of evil paths, yet the Buddha within deluded thought transforms and brings forth a subtle image. The hand draws the thread of deluded thought; the needle pierces the bright plain silk; needle by needle one sees the Dharma-body, thought by thought one accomplishes right awakening. In this converging condition one suddenly sees the inconceivable. So one knows the Dharma-realm is empty, and the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. I vow that all living beings, from the needle and thread of deluded thought, may thought by thought see the Dharma-body and none fail to become buddhas.
Praise of Vairocana Buddha

At the tip of a single hair he manifests a subtle image, like a flower in the sky, like a reflection in a mirror. The more he would hide, the more he shows; hardly has he gathered it in when he lets it out. So one knows that my teacher's light is measureless.
Praise of Contemplating the Buddha

I bow my head to the pure Dharma-body, measureless gathering of light, most excellent king of lotuses, therefore named the holy among the holy. Utterly still ocean of extinction, he responds and manifests a subtle image, sitting upright in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, gathering and transforming living beings. With one mind he universally seals the minds of all living beings; hence living beings' minds are the Tathāgata of suchness. Mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are originally without difference. Seeing the mind is seeing the Buddha; recollecting the Buddha is recollecting the mind. At one sight of his surpassing countenance one awakens to the nature of reality. Therefore from the tip of a single hair he manifests this rare thing. Bowing and recollecting, taking refuge for a moment, one at once gains the eternal fruit.
Praise of the Tathāgata Walking in Meditation
